newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Havel could be back at work in weeks - Czech PM.
newsitem.headline: Havel could be back at work in weeks - Czech PM.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel underwent successful lung surgery on Monday and was expected to return to work within weeks, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said.

"The only information that I have is that the surgery was successful this morning and that the forecast prognosis is positive," Klaus told a news conference on the sidelines of a summit of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Lisbon.
Asked when Havel would return to work, Klaus said: "I expect a matter of weeks."
Czech surgeons excised a small malignant tumour from Havel on Monday and removed half of his lung.
Havel, a 60-year-old who has smoked heavily since his youth, was admitted to hospital a week ago afterfailing to throw off a persistent illness. His wife Olga, 62, died in January of cancer.
Earlier in Prague, Havel's spokesman Ladislav Spacek had said that the operation had gone without complications.
Surgeon Pavel Pafko, who led the operating team, said Havel could be back at work soon. The convalescence period for a non-manual worker was about six weeks, he said.
Havel, a small, nervous man, is widely admired at home and internationally for his struggle against communism. He spent years in prison in the late 1970s and 1980s.

In late 1989 the dissident playwright proclaimed the end of communism to hundreds of thousands of cheering Czechs in Prague's Wenceslas Square as the non-violent "Velvet Revolution" swept him into the presidency of what was Czechoslovakia.
Under his leadership Czechoslovak democracy, twice extinguished this century by Nazi Germany and the Communists, was restored and the country set about rebuilding a market economy.

In late 1992 he resigned rather than preside over the division of the nation into separate Czech and Slovak republics. But early the following year parliament re-elected him to a five-year term as president of the Czech Republic alone.
His relations with Prime Minister Klaus, a fervent free marketeer, have at times been strained.
